blocks.text: Appendix. In the preceding article we mentioned the Mishnah according to which one who by a vow forbids himself the enjoyment of צחנה may also not eat טרית טרופה. According to all the commentaries, צחנה is said to be small fish; only, as some think, these are crushed and mixed together, or, as others think, whole and salted, among which, however, crushed ones are occasionally also found. Even טרית טרופה is explained by Rashi (on A. Sara 35b), as mentioned earlier, as small fish; accordingly we would venture the following conjecture. טרית has a double meaning: in some passages cited in the preceding article the name denotes the large tunny Triton, whereas in our Mishnah passage it denotes the small anchovy species which in Aristotle (loc. cit. 9, 25, 8) and in Aelian (loc. cit. 6, 32) is called Θρίσσα [thrissa]. The word is derived from Θρίξ [thrix] "hair", because this small fish has hair-fine bones, and perhaps the טרית טרופה was prepared from this small fish, which is why it was regarded as equivalent to צחנה. It may be noted, moreover, that גולרנא too denotes both a large sea fish (§. 352) and a small species of fish (§. 332).
What strengthens us in our conjecture is that Rashi also translates צחנתא (A. Sara 39a) as herring (§. 328), and, as is well known, the anchovy belongs to the herring family.

בנותא, also בינותא (B. Kama 19b). This fish too belongs to the tunny family and is thus a clean fish, although [p. 257] nothing explicit is said in the Talmud regarding the cleanness of this fish. Some proverbs extant about this fish illustrate various points of its natural history. The first proverb runs: בינותא אכרסה חקלה "The bonito weighs according to the size of its belly", and the buyer is advised first to have the entrails of the fish removed and then to buy the flesh (B. mez. 79b). In fact the bonito (Pelamys Sarda, the Amia of the ancients) has a very long gall bladder (Voigt l. c. 3, p. 195), and this, together with the other inedible parts of the interior, may therefore add not insignificantly to its weight*).
It seems to have been hung up to dry in the air, for a second proverb runs: "In the presence of one who has a hanged man in his family, do not call out: ""Hang up the bonito for me!""" (ibid. 59b).
In that first passage it is related that a donkey, out of hunger, devoured a bonito.

In another passage (Beza 28a) it is reported how someone received 7 bonitos as a gift, five of which, however, another person took from him; this caused resentment in the former, but the friendship of the two was not thereby disturbed. From this at least it follows that the bonito must be a valuable fish, which is indeed the case; its flesh is excellent (Voigt loc. cit.).

In medicine it is used against diseases of the spleen. One roasts it on smith's coals, then quenches them, and eats the fish together with the water (Gittin 69b). On ביניתא דבי כרבא, which the Tosafot erroneously explain as a fish, see §. 458.

In Chulin 66b and in the parallel passage A. Sara 39a, five species of fish are placed side by side, of which it is stated that they are clean because they possess scales and fins in the water but sometimes lose them when they are taken out of the water, i.e. because these are not firmly attached, they can easily lose them through some accident or other. This single statement, of course, cannot greatly advance the identification of the fish. These fish are called: 1) אקונם, 2) אפונם, 3) כספתיאת, 4) אכספטיאם and [p. 258] 5) אטונם. In that parallel passage the third fish is called כטספטיים and the fifth אוטנם; the latter word is incorrect (§. 317), but even for אטונם, טונם is more correct, and so the remaining names too—quite apart from the fact that those variants already render the present spelling doubtful—are probably written corruptly as well, whereby the identification is indeed made more difficult, but at the same time wide scope is left for conjecture. Rashi considers all those names to be Persian; but אטונם is evidently the Greek Θύννος [thynnos] (§. 317), and the other names too betray Greek origin. We shall now attempt to determine those four names, since אטונם has already been dealt with earlier.

The first of those five fish is the אקונם (Chulin 66b). I conjecture that it is the Greek Ὄρκυνος [orkynos], by which Aristotle (loc. cit. 5, 9, 5) denotes a large species of tunny*). Pliny (loc. cit. 32, 11, 53) says: The Orcynus is the largest species of pelamys and does not, like the Triton, return into the Sea of Azov (Maeotis); with age it increases in value**). Because of its very long pectoral fins it is, as is well known, also called Alalonga.

The second of those five fish is the אפונם (Chulin 66b). It belongs to the clean fish because its scales and fins could have fallen off through some accident or other after it was taken out of the sea.

Following the etymology of אקונם in the preceding [p. 259] article, we would also compare אפונם with Ὀρφῶς [orphōs], whose diminutive is Ὄρφιον [orphion]. In Aelian (Thierg. 5, 18) the fish is called Ὀρφός [orphos], for which Ὀρφανός [orphanos] is also written. Perhaps, then, אפונם means the orf, though here, admittedly, we must limit ourselves to conjecture only.

The third of those five fish is the כספתיאה (Chulin 66b), a word which Mussaphia explains as כוססםום, i.e. Κόσσυφος [kossyphos]. This fish lives under rocks and is called Κόττυφος [kottyphos] in Aristot. (loc. cit. 8, 17, 1), Turdus in Plin. (loc. cit. 9, 15, 20).
